questions.content: Describe two long-term causes of tension between the Great Powers of Europe before 1914. Give a detail to support each cause. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] First long-term cause identified, e.g. the alliance system, the naval and arms race, imperial rivalry or nationalism in the Balkans.
[1] Accurate supporting detail, e.g. the Triple Alliance of 1882 between Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy; the Franco-Russian alliance of 1894; the Entente Cordiale of 1904.
[1] A second, different long-term cause identified.
[1] Accurate supporting detail, e.g. the launch of HMS Dreadnought in 1906 and the Anglo-German naval race; the Moroccan crises of 1905 and 1911; Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia in 1908.
Accept other valid causes and accurate detail.

questions.content: Explain how the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 led to a European war by early August 1914. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] The Archduke, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was shot by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist who wanted Bosnia freed from Austro-Hungarian rule.
[1] Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and, in early July, received Germany's promise of support (often called the blank cheque).
[1] Austria-Hungary sent Serbia an ultimatum in late July, and Serbia did not accept every demand.
[1] Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914.
[1] Russia mobilised to defend Serbia, and through the alliances Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August.
[1] Germany invaded Belgium and Britain, which had promised to protect Belgian neutrality, declared war on Germany on 4 August.
Accept other accurate, relevant points of causation.

questions.content:
Source A: a diary entry (an imagined diary written for this paper, by a London office clerk; treat it as a genuine diary for the questions)

Wednesday 5 August 1914. The news was pinned up in the window of the newspaper office late last night: we are at war with Germany. A great crowd had gathered outside the palace gates by the time I walked home, singing and waving flags. The young men at the office talk of it as an adventure that will be over by Christmas, and Mr Hallam, the manager, has already offered to keep the jobs open for any man who joins up. I confess I felt proud of the crowds. Yet my mother cried when I read her the headlines, and I did not sleep. I wonder whether the people cheering have thought what a war between great nations will really mean.

Assess the value and limitations of Source A for a historian studying how people in Britain reacted to the outbreak of war in August 1914. Refer to the origin, purpose and content of the source. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Origin: it is a private diary entry written by a London office clerk on 5 August 1914, the day after Britain declared war.
[1] Purpose: a personal record not meant for publication, so the writer is likely to be honest about his feelings.
[1] Value: it shows mixed reactions, excitement and pride in the crowds alongside worry, which gives a balanced picture.
[1] Value: the content supports what is known from other evidence, e.g. flag-waving crowds and the belief that the war would be over by Christmas.
[1] Limitation: it records the view of one person in London, so it cannot represent the whole of Britain, such as workers in other places, women or those who opposed the war.
[1] Limitation: it covers only the first days of the war and says nothing about later experience or about the causes of war.
Accept other valid points about origin, purpose, value and limitation.

questions.content:
Source B: a table of statistics (constructed for this paper; all figures are approximate and rounded)

Approximate size of the peacetime army of five European powers, 1914

Russia: about 1,400,000 soldiers
Germany: about 800,000 soldiers
France: about 700,000 soldiers
Austria-Hungary: about 450,000 soldiers
Britain: about 250,000 soldiers

Note: Germany and Austria-Hungary were allies. France and Russia were allies, and Britain had agreements with both of them.

Source C: an editorial from an imagined newspaper in a European great power, 1913 (written for this paper)

Our neighbours add new regiments and new warships every year. We cannot be the only nation to sit idle. A country that does not guard its borders invites others to test them. Let every citizen support the new army law, however heavy the cost, for peace is kept only by those strong enough to defend it. Weakness, not strength, is the surest road to war.

Compare what Source B and Source C suggest about attitudes to military strength in Europe before 1914. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Source B shows that several powers kept large armies, with Russia the largest and Germany and France next.
[1] Source C argues for expanding the army and says strength is needed for safety, so both sources show that military strength was seen as important.
[1] Difference in type: Source B gives neutral figures, whereas Source C is an opinion that tries to persuade readers.
[1] A supported judgement, e.g. Source C helps explain why the numbers in Source B were so high, but it reflects only one country's view and Source B does not show navies or reserves.
Accept other valid comparisons.

questions.content:
Source D: a letter from an imagined British soldier to his mother, France, September 1916 (written for this paper)

Dear Mum, thank you for the socks and the cake, which the lads and I shared in the trench. When we joined up in 1914 we thought it would all be done by Christmas. Two years on, three of the boys from our street are gone and I have stopped counting the rest. It rains most days and the mud is everywhere. I will not write about the worst of it, because I do not want you to lie awake. I only want to come home and sit in our kitchen again. Keep my cap for me. Your loving son, Tom.

What can you learn from Source D about how the experience of the war and attitudes to it changed between 1914 and 1916? Support your answer with details from the source. (4 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] In 1914 there was optimism, as the volunteers believed the war would be over by Christmas.
[1] By 1916 the soldier is weary and wants only to go home, shown by 'I only want to come home'.
[1] The war has brought heavy losses, as three boys from his street are gone and he has stopped counting the rest.
[1] Trench life was harsh (rain and mud), and he hides the worst details from his family.
Accept other valid inferences supported by the source.

questions.content: Explain two consequences of the First World War. In your answer, give a separate paragraph for each consequence and use accurate historical terms. (6 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] First consequence clearly identified, e.g. the loss of millions of lives, the collapse of empires, the Treaty of Versailles of 1919, the Russian Revolution of 1917 or changes in women's roles.
[1] Accurate and specific supporting knowledge for the first consequence, e.g. the Austro-Hungarian, German, Russian and Ottoman empires collapsed; Germany lost territory and had to pay reparations.
[1] The first consequence is explained, showing how or why it resulted from the war.
[1] A second, different consequence clearly identified.
[1] Accurate and specific supporting knowledge for the second consequence, e.g. some women in Britain gained the vote in 1918; the League of Nations was created.
[1] The second consequence is explained, and the answer is organised in clear paragraphs with appropriate terminology.
Accept other valid consequences.

questions.content:
'The alliance system was the main cause of the outbreak of the First World War in 1914.'

To what extent do you agree with this statement? Use your own knowledge and refer to other causes in your answer. (10 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
[1] Explains how the alliances divided Europe into two armed camps, e.g. the Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente.
[1] Shows that alliances turned a conflict in the Balkans into a general war, e.g. Russia backing Serbia, Germany backing Austria-Hungary, and France supporting Russia.
[1] Considers militarism and the arms race, e.g. the naval race and the German Schlieffen Plan, which required a rapid attack on France.
[1] Considers imperial and economic rivalry, e.g. the Moroccan crises of 1905 and 1911.
[1] Considers nationalism in the Balkans, e.g. Serbian ambitions, the annexation of Bosnia in 1908 and the assassination at Sarajevo as the trigger.
[1] Considers the decisions of governments in July 1914, e.g. Germany's support for Austria-Hungary and the ultimatum to Serbia.
[1] Weighs the importance of alliances against at least one other cause, e.g. alliances spread the war but did not by themselves start it.
[1] Shows links between causes, e.g. the arms race and alliances increased each other's effects.
[1] Reaches a clear, supported judgement about the extent of agreement.
[1] Accurate dates, names and terms are used, and the answer is organised logically.
Accept other valid arguments, provided they are supported by accurate evidence.
